prompt: Which of the six questions comes first?
hint: It decides most choices on its own.

choices.text: What does it cost at this workload?
choices.why: Price comes last, once the other five say what to multiply.

choices.text: What is the access pattern?
choices.why: Right. How data is written and read narrows everything else.

choices.text: Who operates it?
choices.why: That is the fifth question.

choices.text: How big does it grow, and how fast?
choices.why: That is the fourth.

prompt: Why does asking the price first choose badly?
hint: Think of BigQuery and a customer's screen.

choices.text: Because prices change faster than access patterns do, so the answer would be out of date by next month
choices.why: They do change, but the reason is about what the price is multiplied by.

choices.text: It picks what the pattern ruled out
choices.why: Right. A cheap per-query store is ruinous for a screen opened a hundred thousand times a day.

choices.text: Because the price pages need an account
choices.why: They are public; lesson 1 read them.

choices.text: Because the cheapest store is the slowest
choices.why: Not in general; the point is about order, not a rule linking price and speed.

prompt: A dashboard of yesterday's sales and a screen showing an order just paid. Which question separates them most?
hint: One of them may be a moment behind.

choices.text: Consistency
choices.why: Right. The paid order must be seen at once; yesterday's sales do not care about the last second.

choices.text: Who operates the store, since a dashboard is the analysts' and the screen is the developers'
choices.why: Ownership differs, but the data's freshness is what separates the stores.

choices.text: Price
choices.why: Price comes after the shape is known.

choices.text: Scale
choices.why: Both can be small; the difference is how fresh the read must be.

prompt: How does Cloud SQL grow, as the scale question describes it?
hint: One writer.

choices.text: By spreading across splits
choices.why: That is Spanner.

choices.text: By slots borrowed for a query
choices.why: That is BigQuery.

choices.text: By a bigger machine, until there is none bigger
choices.why: Right. Read replicas add readers, not writers.

choices.text: By adding nodes to a cluster while writes are spread among them
choices.why: Bigtable grows that way; Cloud SQL has one writer.

prompt: Which branch of the tree is Memorystore on?
hint: Under a millisecond.

choices.text: Transactions and joins
choices.why: That is Cloud SQL and AlloyDB.

choices.text: Events that never stop
choices.why: That is Pub/Sub.

choices.text: Questions over all of history
choices.why: That is BigQuery.

choices.text: The same reads, sub-millisecond
choices.why: Right, and it is never the store of record.

prompt: Why is Pub/Sub not a store in the usual sense?
hint: Where do the events end up?

choices.text: It keeps a message only until it is acknowledged or its retention runs out
choices.why: Right. It is where events travel; Cloud Storage and BigQuery are where they are kept.

choices.text: It holds no data at all, not even for a second, and passes every message straight through
choices.why: It holds messages until they are acknowledged, up to its retention.

choices.text: It is too expensive to keep data in
choices.why: The reason is what it does with a message, not its price.

choices.text: It has no emulator
choices.why: It has one; lesson 19 used it.

prompt: An analyst asks BigQuery for the order placed a minute ago and does not find it. What does the tree's table say?
hint: Read the consistency column.

choices.text: BigQuery lost the order and the load has to be repeated from the start
choices.why: Nothing was lost; the warehouse answers as of what reached it.

choices.text: The warehouse answers as of its last load or stream, so this was the wrong store to ask
choices.why: Right. The store of record for a fresh order is Cloud SQL.

choices.text: The query needs a partition filter
choices.why: A filter changes the bill, not what data exists.

choices.text: The analyst needs more slots
choices.why: More slots answer faster about the same data.

prompt: Why did Quitanda not choose Spanner for its orders?
hint: Which question did not ask for it?

choices.text: Spanner cannot run transactions
choices.why: It runs them, across regions; that is its point.

choices.text: One writer carries the business with years to spare, so that scale would be paid for and not used
choices.why: Right. Decided by scale.

choices.text: Spanner has no emulator
choices.why: It has one; lesson 9 used it.

choices.text: Spanner is not available in São Paulo
choices.why: Availability was not the reason given.

prompt: Where do carts live, and what removes the abandoned ones?
hint: A cart is one key, read often, then forgotten.

choices.text: In Cloud SQL, with a nightly `DELETE` job run by Cloud Composer
choices.why: It would work and fill the business's database with rows nobody keeps.

choices.text: In Memorystore, evicted when memory is full
choices.why: Eviction is not a decision about which carts are abandoned.

choices.text: In Firestore, deleted by a time-to-live policy
choices.why: Right. TTL deletes are billed at the cheap delete rate, with nothing to schedule.

choices.text: In BigQuery, partitioned by day
choices.why: A cart is one key read in milliseconds, not a scan.

prompt: The click stream feeds three stores. Which one answers "this customer's last fifty clicks, now"?
hint: Keyed by customer and a reversed timestamp.

choices.text: BigQuery
choices.why: It holds the aggregates, and answers in seconds.

choices.text: Bigtable
choices.why: Right. Lesson 11's row key makes it one range read.

choices.text: Cloud Storage
choices.why: It keeps the raw events in files, read in bulk.

choices.text: Pub/Sub, by seeking back fifty messages on the customer's own subscription
choices.why: Pub/Sub has no per-customer read, and a seek moves a whole subscription.

prompt: Cloud SQL and BigQuery disagree about an order's total. Which is right?
hint: One rule over all of them.

choices.text: BigQuery, because it is newer
choices.why: It is a copy, as of the last change stream it received.

choices.text: Whichever was written last
choices.why: The copies are written after the store of record, by definition.

choices.text: Neither, until somebody reconciles them
choices.why: The rule settles it without a reconciliation.

choices.text: Cloud SQL, the store of record for orders
choices.why: Right. Every other copy is derived from it.

prompt: Firestore bills $0.045 per 100,000 documents read. The screen is opened 3,000,000 times a month and each opening reads ten orders. What do the reads cost a month, in dollars?
hint: Count documents, not queries.

prompt: Why is the number of lookups absent from Cloud SQL's lines in `my_orders.py`?
hint: What does the instance bill?

choices.text: The program forgot it
choices.why: It is left out on purpose; the price does not depend on it.

choices.text: It bills by the hour
choices.why: Right. Three million lookups or three, the same bill.

choices.text: Lookups are free below a quota
choices.why: There is no per-query charge to have a quota on.

choices.text: Because the cache in front of it answers every one of the lookups, so none ever reaches the database
choices.why: No cache was priced in this comparison.

prompt: BigQuery came out near Cloud SQL's price for the screen. Why is it still ruled out?
hint: The second question.

choices.text: Latency: each lookup is a job that takes a second or more
choices.why: Right. Latency rules it out before the price is read.

choices.text: It has no index on the customer
choices.why: Clustering would help the bytes, not the seconds.

choices.text: It cannot store 50 GiB
choices.why: It stores far more.

choices.text: The first free tebibyte of the month runs out on the very first day of every month
choices.why: The free TiB was already subtracted; the problem is speed.

prompt: A team whose orders already live in Cloud SQL adds the "my orders" screen. What does it cost them?
hint: The machine is already running.

choices.text: About $329 a month
choices.why: That is the instance alone, which they already pay for.

choices.text: About $21 a month
choices.why: That is Firestore's price.

choices.text: Close to nothing: an index on the customer and the date, on a machine already paid for
choices.why: Right. The cheapest store is often the one already running for the workload next door.

choices.text: A second instance for the extra queries, with its own standby in another zone
choices.why: A screen of indexed lookups is a sliver of the machine.

prompt: A `jobs` table polled every second by workers. What does PostgreSQL do with every finished job?
hint: An update in PostgreSQL.

choices.text: Nothing; the row is updated in place
choices.why: PostgreSQL writes a new row version and leaves the old one.

choices.text: It leaves a dead row behind for vacuum
choices.why: Right, so a busy queue table bloats and the polls slow down.

choices.text: It moves the row to an archive table
choices.why: Nothing moves it unless somebody writes that.

choices.text: It sends a message to Pub/Sub
choices.why: That is the cure, not what the database does.

prompt: A Bigtable table's row key starts with the event's timestamp. What happens?
hint: Where does every new write land?

choices.text: Writes spread evenly because timestamps are unique
choices.why: Unique is not spread: they are all adjacent, at the end of the key space.

choices.text: Reads of one customer get faster
choices.why: One customer's events are scattered through time.

choices.text: Every write lands on the node holding the end of the key space
choices.why: Right. A hotspot, while the rest of the cluster idles.

choices.text: Bigtable refuses the table when it is created, because a timestamp cannot start a row key
choices.why: It accepts any key; the design is yours.

prompt: An application writes its rows into BigQuery one `UPDATE` at a time. Which problem does the lesson name?
hint: What is each DML statement?

choices.text: Each statement is a job that rewrites storage, and concurrent DML per table queues
choices.why: Right, and its keys are not enforced either.

choices.text: BigQuery refuses `UPDATE` statements
choices.why: It runs them; it is just built for the opposite.

choices.text: The rows cannot be read afterwards, by anyone, until the end of the day
choices.why: They can; the trouble is in the writing.

choices.text: It is free, so nobody notices
choices.why: DML is billed like a query, by bytes processed.

prompt: Match each Quitanda workload to its store.
hint: One store of record each, plus a cache.

prompt: Put the six questions in the order the lesson asks them.
hint: The price is last.
items: How fast must an answer come?
What consistency does the reader need?
How big, and how fast does it grow?
What does it cost, at this workload?

prompt: One store of ___ per fact, and every other copy derived from it.
hint: The store that is right by definition.

prompt: A new workload: a fraud check that must read a customer's last hour of payments in under ten milliseconds, a hundred thousand times a second. Which branch?
hint: One row key, huge throughput.

choices.text: Bigtable
choices.why: Right. A row key of customer and reversed time, read as one range.

choices.text: BigQuery, partitioned by hour so that each check reads only the last partition
choices.why: Seconds per query, and a hundred thousand of them a second.

choices.text: Cloud SQL
choices.why: One writer and one machine at that rate is the edge of the branch.

choices.text: Cloud Storage
choices.why: Files read in bulk, tens of milliseconds each.
